passages.original: Verum non sine labore didicisti tuam sapientiani fatuam, Plato : quem mundus retinere non poterat, mundi sapientiam insequentem, per diversarum nationum, et gentium, regionumque partes, infinitis aerumnis innumerisque peragrando laboribus. Nec tamen fatuissimæ sapientiae finem, qui est summum bonum, ad quod te naturae movebat intentio, in orbe universo reperire scivisti : quem sancti hi rustici hanc fugientes invenerunt in eremis latitantes. Attende et tu, fatuorum sapicntium princeps, Aristoteles : etsi fueris, absque dubitatione, prodigium grandeque miraculum in tota natura : cui pene vi, detur infusum, quidquid naturaliter est capax humanum genus : quoniam sapientia mundi, stultitia est apud Deum (I Cor.
passages.english: But not without toil did you learn your foolish wisdom, Plato: you whom the world could not hold, pursuing the wisdom of the world, by travelling through the parts of diverse nations, peoples and regions with endless hardships and countless labours. And yet you did not know how to find, in the whole world, the end of your most foolish wisdom, which is the highest good, toward which the striving of nature moved you: [the end] which these holy rustics, fleeing that [wisdom], found while hiding in the deserts. Pay attention, you too, Aristotle, prince of the foolish wise: even if you were, without doubt, a prodigy and a great marvel in all of nature, into whom there seems to have been poured almost whatever the human race is naturally capable of; since the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God (1 Cor.
passages.notes: "sapientiani" and "sapicntium" are scanning errors for "sapientiam" and "sapientium". "cui pene vi, detur infusum" appears garbled; read as "cui pene videtur infusum" ("into whom almost ... seems to have been poured"). The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the scriptural reference (1 Cor. 3), which continues in the following text.
